title: Exposure to grass pollen--but not birch pollen--affects lung function in Swedish children.
ehr_evidence: Children belonging to the Swedish birth cohort BAMSE underwent clinical examination including lung-function testing and blood sampling for measuring serum immunoglobulin E (IgE) against common airborne and food allergens (ImmunoCAP System; Phadia AB, Uppsala, Sweden) at eight (N = 1838) and sixteen years of age (N = 2063) (year 2003 – 2004 and 2011 –2012, respectively).
summary: Investigation of the effect of grass and birch pollen exposure on lung function in 8- and 16-year-old children from the Swedish BAMSE birth cohort.
key_findings: Increased grass pollen exposure the day before testing was associated with reduced FEV1 in 8-year-olds (-32.4 ml; 95% CI: -50.6 to -14.2 per 3 pollen counts/m³).
The negative effect was stronger in children sensitized to pollen allergens (FEV1: -41.6 ml; 95% CI: -68.3 to -14.8).
No associations were found for birch or other pollen exposure in 8-year-olds.
Pollen exposure was not related to lung function in 16-year-olds.
captured_features: ambient air pollution levels (ozone, NO2, PM10, PM2.5)
demographic and clinical covariates (sex, age, height, allergic heredity)
data_source_type: birth cohort and environmental monitoring stations
population: children aged 8 and 16 years from the BAMSE birth cohort in Stockholm, Sweden
exposure_domain: airborne pollen and ambient air pollution
limitations: Lung function tests were not conducted during the peak summer pollen season, limiting assessment of acute exposure.
Lack of IgG/IgG4 data to evaluate tolerance development.
Potential confounding by differences in indoor/outdoor time between age groups.
Relatively low pollen concentrations during study years.
